bio.en: Claire Butler was Figma's 10th employee and first marketing hire, leading its original launch, go-to-market, branding, and positioning, and continues to lead go-to-market and bottom-up growth.
bio.zh: Claire Butler 是 Figma 的第 10 号员工和首位营销员工，领导了其最初发布、进入市场、品牌与定位，并持续负责进入市场与自下而上的增长。

summary.en: Claire gives the first in-depth look at how Figma grew and continues to grow, sharing a two-part go-to-market strategy: winning individual contributors' love, then enabling them to spread the product internally. She offers vivid stories from executing that strategy and how other teams can apply it. The conversation is dense with go-to-market wisdom for bottom-up, IC-led products.
summary.zh: Claire 首次深入展示了 Figma 如何增长并持续增长的：她分享了两步进入市场策略——先赢得个人贡献者（IC）的喜爱，再让他们在组织内自发传播产品。她用生动故事讲述了执行该策略的过程，以及其他团队如何借鉴。对话充满了针对自下而上、由 IC 驱动产品的市场进入智慧。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: We had Coda. They were our first user, and they were based in Palo Alto. Dylan and I drove down and demoed the product to them, and they were the first ones. Their designer, Jeremy was like, "Yes, we'll take this on full time." And I remember we were both like, "What? Really? You will?" That was the first person who said yes to us. And so, we were so excited. This was a huge milestone. We were just so stoked. And then we got back to the office, and I think Dylan gets a text from Jeremy being like, "Oh yeah, I tried to share this with Philippe, my engineer, and he can't get the file to open, so I guess we can't use it." And we're like, "What is it? What happened?" Finally got someone. And I remember Dylan was like, "Everybody drop everything. We have to fix this." (00:00:37): And after some looking at the servers and things, they were like, "Nothing's wrong." And then they realized there's a problem with Philippe's MacBook. And Evan down only had a car, so Dylan had to drive Evan down to Palo Alto to fix the MacBook of Philippe just to get them to use the product.

turns.zh: 您长期以来一直在我的愿望清单上，所以我很高兴终于能和您聊天了。你是 Figma 的第 10 名员工，该公司现在价值数百亿美元，具体取决于你看的估值，可能还有数千名员工。我也不知道，但是很多很多。您甚至在产品推出之前就加入了。因此，我想问一百万个问题，关于 Figma 是如何发展的以及其中涉及的所有内容。我很好奇在 Figma 的早期是什么样的。脑海中是否浮现出一段滑稽、有趣、有趣、有形的记忆，就像早期在 Figma 工作的感觉一样？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, totally. No, that's a good question. We were right downtown on New Montgomery and Minna, and I think the thing that sticks out to me is actually two competing stories that talk about just how much at that time you'd oscillate between these really high-level strategic decisions and then total current work. (00:04:50): So my first day at Figma, I come into the office and we're going through some stuff. There's like 10 of us in the office, we're chatting, and I look at some of the plans, some of the things they're working on, and I see that they were actually had some branding and positioning and things that the products, Figma, was going to be named Summit, that was the name. So the company was going to be Figma, and then the product suite, the product design tool was going to be Summit with the idea that eventually we'll have other tools and that could be like mountaintop or I don't know what the rule, they had a whole thing around the different things that could be for the future product set. (00:05:27): And I remember my first day, I had an immediate reaction of like, " We cannot make this thing Summit. That's not going to work. We can't have two brands. Summit's not ownable, we can't build equity and multiple things. That's just never going to work. We kind of have to just stick with one." And I think Figma is ownable and makes sense and we should just go with Figma. So we kind of should probably kill the Summit thing. And Dylan said to me, he was like, "Oh, that's interesting. How about you make a presentation and present it to everyone tomorrow?" And so I did that. I was like, "Oh, okay, I guess this is what I'm doing the rest of the day." So I went and made a little presentation about how we couldn't build all this equity in two places and all of the things, and then the next day we decided to kill that name. (00:06:05): And so we went with Figma for the name of the product instead of Summit. And that's how fast things moved, right? And how much you just ran with it and how to ownership. I compare that to the first meetup we had, which was probably just 10 people in the office, honestly. But I remember I was in charge of that, so I had to get all the food and everything there, and I just Instacarted some things and ordered some pizza, but I'd forgotten ice. And so I had to go walk down to the nearest corner store, which was three blocks away or something, and get ice. And I got four bags. And I remember I was walking down the street down probably third street with three bags of ice and it was really heavy. And I remember thinking, "This is so hard. This is so heavy. I can't carry all this ice." And it's just like that's... I did that too probably the next week. (00:06:50): And so, I think it was just this oscillation between like, "Oh, we're making these high level strategic decisions and someone else has to go by the ice." So that's what it was like at Figma in the early days.
turns.zh: 是的，完全可以。不，这是个好问题。我们就在新蒙哥马利和明纳的市中心，我认为最让我印象深刻的是两个相互竞争的故事，它们讲述了当时你会在这些真正的高层战略决策和当前的总体工作之间摇摆不定。 (00:04:50)：我在 Figma 的第一天，我走进办公室，我们正在处理一些事情。我们办公室里大约有 10 个人，我们正在聊天，我查看了一些计划，他们正在做的一些事情，我发现他们实际上有一些品牌和定位以及产品，Figma，将被命名为 Summit，这就是名字。所以公司将成为Figma，然后是产品套件，产品设计工具将成为Summit，我们的想法是最终我们将拥有其他工具，这可能就像山顶，或者我不知道规则是什么，他们围绕可能适用于未来产品集的不同事物有一整套东西。 (00:05:27)：我记得我第一天的反应是，“我们不能把这件事做成 Summit。那是行不通的。我们不能有两个品牌。Summit 是不可拥有的，我们不能建立股权和多种东西。那是永远行不通的。我们必须坚持一个。”我认为 Figma 是可拥有的并且有意义，我们应该选择 Figma。所以我们应该取消峰会的事情。迪伦对我说，“哦，这很有趣。你明天做一个演示并向大家展示怎么样？”所以我就这么做了。我当时想，“哦，好吧，我想这就是我今天剩下的时间要做的事情。”所以我做了一个小演示，说明我们如何无法在两个地方和所有事情上建立所有这些股权，然后第二天我们决定取消这个名字。 (00:06:05)：因此我们使用 Figma 作为产品名称，而不是 Summit。这就是事情发展的速度，对吗？以及你用它跑了多少以及如何拥有它。我将其与我们的第一次聚会进行了比较，老实说，办公室里可能只有 10 个人。但我记得我负责这件事，所以我必须把所有的食物和所有的东西都拿到那里，我只是用 Instacarted 一些东西并点了一些披萨，但我忘记了冰。所以我不得不步行到最近的街角商店，距离三个街区之类的地方，买冰块。我有四袋。我记得我带着三袋冰沿着可能是第三条街的街道走，它真的很重。我记得我当时想：“这太难了。这太重了。我无法携带所有这些冰。”就像那样......我可能在下周也这样做了。 (00:06:50)：所以，我认为这只是在“哦，我们正在做出这些高层战略决策，而其他人必须采取行动”之间的摇摆。这就是 Figma 早期的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. That's almost a metaphor. Someone's got to go carry the ice.
turns.zh: 那真是难以置信。这几乎是一个比喻。得有人去搬冰块。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Almost got to the ice for the meetup. Yep.
turns.zh: 差点就去冰场参加聚会了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: Summit 太有趣了，我不知道那是 [听不清 00:07:09]-

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: That wasn't a good name. So if you liked that better, I'm sorry because I killed that.
turns.zh: 那不是一个好名字。所以，如果你更喜欢那个，我很抱歉，因为我杀了它。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: The name change or...
turns.zh: 改名或者...

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: The first day. No, that was literally my first day.
turns.zh: 第一天。不，那确实是我的第一天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first day.
turns.zh: 第一天。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: No, no, no. That was my first day and my second day. Not even kidding. My first day, I made the recommendation, the second day, give the presentation and the decision was made.
turns.zh: 不，不，不。那是我的第一天和第二天。甚至不是开玩笑。第一天，我提出了建议，第二天，进行了演示并做出了决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I was going to ask you what the most stressful memory of early days Figma was. I'm guessing it's the same story.
turns.zh: 哇。我想问你 Figma 早期最有压力的记忆是什么。我猜这是同一个故事。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: It's not actually. So I think the most stressful thing, I was thinking about this, was when we launched out of stealth. So I come into Figma, I had lots of experience. I'd been in another startup before that, I launched stuff, but I was still kind of junior. I had done these things, but I didn't have a ton of cycles, and I never ran the whole thing from like, okay, messaging and positioning. This was a forcing function for us to do our messaging and positioning. And I remember there was more than one day where we locked ourselves in a conference room and I made Dylan and show at the time have this positioning up on the big screen and made them agree on it word for word. We'd just never done that before. But then I'd also never run PR press and all of a sudden, I had to run press and PR. (00:08:36): And I think the hardest part there and the most stressful part was I didn't have anyone to talk to. It was just me. And I didn't at the time have enough cycles to have the confidence that the decisions I was making were the right ones. And so it was hard not to second guess myself sometimes in that position. And I think that's some of the hardest times of being at a startup, especially when you're the only marketer, the only go-to-market person is, you don't have anyone to talk to, to like got check stuff with. And so it does take this immense confidence in yourself, but that's stressful when you don't have the cycles. And so that was very stressful for me for sure.
turns.zh: 其实不是。所以我认为最有压力的事情，我在想这个，是当我们从隐身状态发射时。所以我进入Figma，我有很多经验。在此之前我曾在另一家初创公司工作过，我推出了一些东西，但我仍然是初级的。我已经做了这些事情，但我没有太多的周期，而且我从来没有从消息传递和定位等方面运行整个事情。这是我们进行消息传递和定位的强制功能。我记得不止一天我们把自己锁在会议室里，我让迪伦和当时的节目在大屏幕上展示了这一定位，并让他们逐字逐句地达成一致。我们以前从未这样做过。但后来我也从来没有管理过公关媒体，突然之间，我不得不管理媒体和公关。 (00:08:36)：我认为最困难的部分和压力最大的部分是我没有人可以交谈。只有我一个人。当时我没有足够的周期来确信我所做的决定是正确的。因此，有时很难不去怀疑自己的处境。我认为这是在初创公司最困难的时期，尤其是当你是唯一的营销人员、唯一的进入市场的人时，你没有人可以交谈，也没有人可以检查东西。因此，这确实需要对自己有极大的信心，但当你没有周期时，就会有压力。所以这对我来说无疑是非常有压力的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you overcome that? Did you find people to work with and run ideas by? Did you just do it and figure it out?
turns.zh: 你是如何克服这个问题的？你是否找到了可以一起工作并管理创意的人？你刚刚做了并弄清楚了吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: I mean, I had Dylan, but we just did it, right? Especially in those early days. I remember there were a couple of freak out moments where I would try to get our VCs to help us. I remember Greylock was helpful at least over there, but ultimately, they help a lot, but they don't know your business as intimately as you do. So at the end of the day, that's something Dylan's really good at is trusting his intuition and gut. And so, he was helpful on the decision making, but then also you just got to go for it. And I think that that's something that I learned at that time that's helped me throughout the rest of my career is building that confidence or that trust in yourself because it wasn't something that I necessarily immediately had.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我有迪伦，但我们只是做到了，对吧？尤其是在早期。我记得有几次我感到惊慌失措的时候，我会尝试让风投来帮助我们。我记得格雷洛克至少在那里提供了帮助，但最终，他们提供了很多帮助，但他们不像您那样熟悉您的业务。所以归根结底，迪伦真正擅长的就是相信自己的直觉和直觉。因此，他对决策很有帮助，但你也必须坚持下去。我认为我当时学到的东西在我余下的职业生涯中帮助我建立了对自己的信心或信任，因为这不是我必须立即拥有的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question I wanted to get into briefly is, you joined Figma really early, became one of the most successful, loved companies in history. What did you see early on that convinced you that Figma was the company to join and ask? Because a lot of people today are looking for places to join and trying to decide what to do. Clearly, you made a good choice. What did you see?
turns.zh: 我想简单讨论的下一个问题是，你们很早就加入 Figma，成为历史上最成功、最受喜爱的公司之一。您早期看到的是什么让您确信 Figma 就是您要加入并询问的公司？因为今天很多人都在寻找加入的地方并试图决定要做什么。显然，你做了一个很好的选择。你看到了什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: So I had been another startup before Figma, a little bit bigger. I think I joined at Series B and then got through on acquisition. And I had a sense that I wanted to do something early. And I'd already made that decision that I wanted to go early stage. So I'll take that decision making part out. But then from there, I was talking to a couple different companies, and when I went to Figma, there were three areas that stood out the most to me. (00:10:36): The first was, it logically made sense. And I know maybe that sounds basic, but I was talking to just a drone company or a SaaS tech, like ad tech company, and I just didn't get it, honestly, it didn't intuitively make sense to me or I didn't understand the technology or something. But at Figma, the basic premise immediately logically clicked for me like, "Oh yeah, I use Google Docs, I use Asana, I use all these online tools. That's so weird. That design's not online. Why isn't it?" (00:11:06): And as a marketer, I'd worked with designers and sent feedback and emails, and that's really inefficient. And it made a ton of sense to me that yes, that should be online and collaborative. So that was the first thing that I was like check the box. And the next one was, I knew people who believed in it. So I got introduced to Dylan via Index. They were an investor at the last company I was at, and Danny Rimer specifically. And my old boss, Greg Smearon, who was an EIR there. And I trusted them a lot and they invested in it. I also met John Lilly. I didn't know who he was. I had to Google him, but he seemed really smart. And when they Googled in, he was very impressive, and he believed in it. So that was great. (00:11:43): And then I think the third thing was, I remember when I was trying to decide, Dylan really didn't take no for answer. He's very persuasive. And I remember he'd calling me and text me and then I'd have all these concerns or things and he would just pick them apart one by one of reasons why they weren't real concerns or things to get over them. And so I think that that was the third thing is, that's just who he was and that's how he is with everything. And so, if that's how with me, that's how he is with any obstacle that he has. And so, when I looked at that, I was just like, "All right, let's give this a go." And I didn't know. I didn't know. I had no idea it would be as big as it is today. So some of it was luck too, for sure. But those are the three things of how I made my decision.
turns.zh: 所以我是 Figma 之前的另一家初创公司，规模更大一些。我想我加入了 B 轮融资，然后完成了收购。我有一种感觉，我想早点做点什么。我已经做出了想要进入早期阶段的决定。所以我会把决策部分排除掉。但从那时起，我与几家不同的公司进行了交谈，当我去 Figma 时，有三个领域对我来说最突出。 (00:10:36)：第一，它在逻辑上是有道理的。我知道也许这听起来很基本，但我只是在与一家无人机公司或 SaaS 技术公司（例如广告技术公司）交谈，但我只是不明白，老实说，它对我来说直观上没有意义，或者我不了解这项技术或其他什么。但在 Figma，基本前提立刻就合乎逻辑地契合了我的需求，比如，“哦，是的，我使用 Google Docs，我使用 Asana，我使用所有这些在线工具。这太奇怪了。那个设计不在网上。为什么不是呢？” (00:11:06)：作为一名营销人员，我与设计师合作并发送反馈和电子邮件，这确实效率很低。对我来说，这很有意义，是的，这应该是在线和协作的。所以这是我想要勾选复选框的第一件事。下一个是，我认识相信这一点的人。所以我是通过 Index 认识迪伦的。他们是我上一家公司的投资者，特别是丹尼·里默。还有我的前老板 Greg Smearon，他是那里的 EIR。我非常信任他们，他们也对此进行了投资。我还认识了约翰·莉莉。我不知道他是谁。我不得不用谷歌搜索他，但他看起来真的很聪明。当他们用谷歌搜索时，他给人留下了深刻的印象，他相信这一点。所以那太好了。 (00:11:43)：然后我认为第三件事是，我记得当我试图做出决定时，迪伦真的没有接受“不”的回答。他很有说服力。我记得他会给我打电话，给我发短信，然后我就有了所有这些担忧或事情，他只是将它们一一挑出来，解释为什么它们不是真正的担忧或需要克服的事情。所以我认为第三件事是，这就是他是谁，这就是他对待一切的方式。所以，如果我是这样的话，那么他遇到任何障碍也是这样。所以，当我看到这个的时候，我就想，“好吧，让我们试试吧。”我不知道。我不知道。我不知道它会像今天这么大。所以当然，其中也有运气的成分。但这是我做出决定的三件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I took away there is, one, you just believe in idea, obviously. Make sure you actually think this could be really big, two is some social proof people you trust really believe in it. In this case, it was really smart investors, they knew. And then the third is, it sounds like you were also just impressed with Dylan.
turns.zh: 所以我得出的结论是，第一，显然你只相信想法。确保你真的认为这可能真的很大，二是你信任的一些社会证明人确实相信它。他们知道，在这种情况下，投资者真的很聪明。第三，听起来你也对迪伦印象深刻。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I believed in him.
turns.zh: 是的，完全可以。我相信他。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you joined Figma before it even launched, it was still in stealth. You joined as the first go-to-market hire. You helped launch Figma, you continue to lead go-to market at Figma. And so this is a good segue to where I want to spend most of our conversation. I essentially want to try to unpack what worked to build Figma into the business that it is today from beginning to even now. You're also there for eight years. So you saw a lot of what worked and didn't work. And so let's start with the beginnings of Figma and the go-to-market motion that you developed and how you actually implemented it. So maybe to start, if you could just talk about just what is a bottom up go-to-market motion? And then you also shared somewhere that Figma has a very unique bottom-up go-to-market motion. So maybe just those two areas, just broadly, what is bottom-up go- to-market motion, and then two, what is unique about Figma's approach?
turns.zh: 所以你在 Figma 推出之前就加入了它，它仍然处于隐秘状态。您作为第一个进入市场的员工加入。您帮助推出了 Figma，您将继续引领 Figma 的市场走向。因此，这是一个很好的延续，我想在我们的大部分谈话中度过。我本质上是想尝试将 Figma 构建成今天的业务，从开始到现在的工作成果都解开出来。你也在那里呆了八年了。所以你看到了很多有效和无效的方法。那么，让我们从Figma 的起源、您开发的上市动议以及您如何实际实施它开始。那么，也许首先，您能否谈谈什么是自下而上的上市动议？然后您还在某处分享了Figma 有一个非常独特的自下而上的上市行动。因此，也许只是这两个领域，从广义上讲，什么是自下而上的上市运动，然后是两个领域，Figma 方法的独特之处是什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: I've reflected back to get to some of these answers. I think in the moment, so much of what we were doing was influenced by gut, by trying to connect with people, listening to them. But when I look back is when I'm like, "Oh, this is a repeatable motion." So when I look back at it, I would say that if I were to define and think about how I define our go-to-market motion, and we've said it, we've called it a lot of things over time. We called it product-led, we called it community-led. The way I think about it now is this bottoms-up motion, that really is focused on ICs. So it's all focused on like, "Okay, so you have this core audience." For us it was designers and they're largely individual contributors, so they're people who are practitioners who are using your tool. For us, it's like eight hours a day. (00:14:17): If you're a designer, you're in it all the time. And they love you, and you build this relationship with them within the product, but it's beyond the product, right? It's also believing what the product can be in the company and the brand. And they love you so much that they're willing to put their social capital and themselves in the line and spread the product throughout whatever their communities are. And the one that's connected the most to revenue is companies. (00:14:45): And so that's where the revenue model really clicks in is you have all these individual contributors who love you, but then they also work at these big companies and these big orgs, and they become these internal champions who spearhead adoption within their organizations and eventually turn into large amounts of revenue. And I think of that as our bottoms-up motion. And that's different from tops-down. And a lot of SaaS is tops-down where you go straight to a VP or an executive buyer, they then agree to buying a tool and then that goes down to their organization. I think with technical tools especially, this becomes really important. The practitioners have to love it. And also, sometimes I wondered as an executive care, you know what I mean, what tools people are using? (00:15:27): And so for Figma, what that looks like and why this is so efficient of a go-to-market motion for us is, we actually didn't have a sales team for the first three years. So all of our revenue, it was paid, but it was all self-serve. And so we'd work with these. We weren't worried about things. I mean, you cared about security, but all of the org features that people need and want when you're working with procurement, we were just focused on technical features for users mostly. And then the individual contributor or maybe the manager would just put them on their credit card. That was the way that things grew. And so there was no sales team for a long time. We did have one eventually, and I'll talk about what that looked like. (00:16:04): But then the second thing was, once we did have a sales team, and even up until now, so much of our revenue and our sales and our MQLs, our marketing qualified leads come from our free tier. So it's people, they're using it, maybe they use it for free. We have a very robust free tier. Maybe they use it for pro, which is on your credit card. And then once it's widespread and they've gained the confidence, then they're ready to bring in sales work with procurement. And they actually come to us and they're like, "Hey, I work at this company. I really want to get my whole company to use it, but security's not letting me. Can you help me unblock it with them?" (00:16:39): We didn't spend that much money, any money really programmatically on paid or programmatic marketing because all of our leads for sales would come in through a form on our website, which was current users either free or pro wanting to upgrade. And at that point, it's a very different sales conversation to unblock someone or to just help them implement Figma when they've already have an internal champion who's bought in, and they're really the one leading and driving the sale within their organization. So I think that that's made us really efficient as like this is a really efficient model and has really powered so much of our growth over time.
turns.zh: 我经过反思，找到了其中一些答案。我认为目前我们所做的很多事情都受到直觉的影响，试图与人们建立联系，倾听他们的意见。但当我回头看时，我会想，“哦，这是一个可重复的动作。”因此，当我回顾它时，我会说，如果我要定义并思考如何定义我们的上市动议，而且我们已经说过了，随着时间的推移，我们已经给它起了很多名字。我们称之为产品主导，我们称之为社区主导。我现在的想法是这种自下而上的运动，真正关注的是 IC。所以一切都集中在“好吧，所以你有这个核心受众”。对我们来说，是设计师，他们主要是个人贡献者，所以他们是使用你的工具的实践者。对我们来说，就像每天八个小时。 (00:14:17)：如果您是设计师，那么您就一直参与其中。他们爱你，你在产品中与他们建立了这种关系，但这超出了产品的范围，对吗？它还相信产品在公司和品牌中的作用。他们非常爱你，以至于他们愿意将他们的社会资本和他们自己投入其中，并将产品传播到他们所在的社区。与收入关系最密切的是公司。 (00:14:45)：这就是收入模式真正起作用的地方，你拥有所有这些爱你的个人贡献者，但他们也在这些大公司和这些大组织中工作，他们成为这些内部冠军，在他们的组织内率先采用，并最终转化为大量收入。我认为这是我们自下而上的动议。这与自上而下不同。很多 SaaS 都是自上而下的，你直接去找副总裁或执行采购员，然后他们同意购买工具，然后再下达到他们的组织。我认为尤其是对于技术工具来说，这变得非常重要。练习者必须热爱它。而且，有时我想知道，作为一名高管，你知道我的意思，人们正在使用什么工具？ (00:15:27)：对于 Figma 来说，这是什么样子的，以及为什么这对我们来说是一个如此有效的进入市场行动，我们实际上在前三年没有销售团队。所以我们所有的收入都是付费的，但都是自助的。所以我们会与这些一起工作。我们并不担心事情。我的意思是，您关心安全性，但是当您进行采购时，人们需要和想要的所有组织功能，我们主要只关注用户的技术功能。然后个人贡献者或者经理可能会把它们记在信用卡上。事情就是这样发展的。因此很长一段时间没有销售团队。我们最终确实有了一个，我会谈谈它是什么样子的。 (00:16:04)：但第二件事是，一旦我们有了销售团队，甚至到现在为止，我们的大部分收入、销售额、MQL、营销合格的潜在客户都来自我们的免费套餐。所以是人，他们正在使用它，也许他们免费使用它。我们有一个非常强大的免费套餐。也许他们将其用于专业版，这是在您的信用卡上。一旦它广泛传播并且他们获得了信心，他们就准备好将销售工作与采购结合起来。他们实际上来找我们，他们说，“嘿，我在这家公司工作。我真的想让我的整个公司都使用它，但安全部门不允许我。你能帮我和他们一起解锁吗？” (00:16:39)：我们并没有花那么多钱，任何真正以程序化方式进行付费或程序化营销的钱，因为我们所有的销售线索都将通过我们网站上的表格进入，该表格是当前用户免费或想要升级的专业用户。到那时，当他们已经有一位内部支持者并且他们确实是组织内领导和推动销售的人时，解锁某人或只是帮助他们实施 Figma 是一种非常不同的销售对话。所以我认为这让我们变得非常高效，因为这是一个非常高效的模型，并且随着时间的推移确实为我们的增长提供了很大的动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Somebody listening to this that has a saying, B2B SaaS companies like, "Oh, okay, I just need to get people to love my product and it's going to be great." And so I want to unpack that just like what you did because it wasn't obviously an accident that people loved Figma. But before we get there, you talked about that there's a unique approach to the way you did bottom up. What do you see as what the typical bottom-up go-to-market motion is that other companies try to play that you think Figma did differently? Is it this obsession with ICs on teams or is there some other element of it?
turns.zh: 有人听过这样的话，B2B SaaS 公司喜欢，“哦，好吧，我只需要让人们喜欢我的产品，它就会很棒。”所以我想像你所做的那样解开它，因为人们喜欢 Figma 显然不是偶然的。但在我们到达那里之前，您谈到了您自下而上的工作方式有一种独特的方法。您认为其他公司尝试采取的典型的自下而上的入市行动与您认为 Figma 的做法有何不同？是团队对 IC 的痴迷还是还有其他因素？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: I think there are other people who do bottoms-up and who do it well. I think for us it's unique because the individual contributor spends so much time in the tool, and it's so important to them. I think about things that we focus on where it might take one click off of someone's workflow, and that seems like a really small update. You have to click one time instead of twice to do something. (00:18:06): When you're a designer and you're in a tool eight hours a day, saving that one click is huge. And so I think the obsession with quality and with craft within the editor for us, for Figma, is maybe the difference. And I think about other go-to-market tools that maybe focus so much on the collaboration side or the product-led of the expansion. And that is a huge part segue, don't get me wrong, but the tool itself, the editor, that's where it all starts and that's what these people love. And then the collaboration is like, yes, it's the thing that's like our differentiator, but it's actually like you stay for the collaboration. You don't want to talk about it or learn about it. Nobody wants talk about collaboration. You just want it to work, right? You care about the tool and that the tool's working well. And so I think that maybe that's the difference is the obsession with the tool itself.
turns.zh: 我认为还有其他人做自下而上的工作并且做得很好。我认为这对我们来说是独一无二的，因为个人贡献者在该工具上花费了大量时间，这对他们来说非常重要。我认为我们关注的事情可能会在某人的工作流程中单击一下，而这似乎是一个非常小的更新。您必须单击一次而不是两次才能执行某项操作。 (00:18:06)：当您是一名设计师并且每天使用工具八小时时，节省一次点击的时间是巨大的。因此，我认为对我们、Figma 来说，编辑器对质量和工艺的痴迷可能就是不同之处。我想到了其他进入市场的工具，这些工具可能非常关注协作方面或以产品为主导的扩展。这是一个很大的部分，不要误会我的意思，但是工具本身，编辑器，这就是一切的开始，这就是这些人所喜欢的。然后合作就像，是的，这就像我们的差异化因素，但实际上就像你留下来进行合作。你不想谈论它或了解它。没有人愿意谈论合作。你只是想让它发挥作用，对吗？您关心该工具并且该工具运行良好。所以我认为也许这就是区别在于对工具本身的痴迷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Yeah, something I learned recently is that multiplayer wasn't even a part of Figma at launch, [inaudible 00:18:56] a year later.
turns.zh: 惊人的。是的，我最近了解到，一年后，[听不清 00:18:56]，多人游戏甚至不是 Figma 发布时的一部分。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: I know. We can talk about that, and we want to know making a decision of when to go to self because we almost didn't because it didn't have multiplayer.
turns.zh: 我知道。我们可以讨论这个，我们想知道何时决定何时进行自我测试，因为我们几乎没有这样做，因为它没有多人游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, let's talk about that.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，我们来谈谈这个吧。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, that was a poor differentiator and we can't not have it, but then we did anyway.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很差的差异化因素，我们不能没有它，但无论如何我们还是这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's take a tangent there actually. Just that decision to go from stealth. So Figma was in stealth three years or four years before [inaudible 00:19:17] idea.
turns.zh: 是的，让我们实际上在那里切线。只是决定从隐身行动。所以 Figma 在 [听不清 00:19:17] 这个想法之前就已经秘密进行了三四年。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Gosh, three, I guess. I think is 2012 that they started, and then we launched in at the end of 2015. So between around there, yeah, around three or four.
turns.zh: 天哪，我猜是三个。我认为他们是在 2012 年开始的，然后我们在 2015 年底推出了。所以在那之间，是的，大约有三到四个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then you joined right before they launched. We're going to come back to what we were talking about, but just what did you see about that decision of now's the time to launch?
turns.zh: 凉爽的。然后你在他们推出之前加入了。我们将回到我们正在讨论的内容，但您对现在发布的决定有何看法？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, I think it was a couple things. So I think the first thing is that the team had been building quietly by themselves in isolation for three years. And that's hard. I think that that was a very real part of the decision to get out of stealth was that people had been building for such a long time. We needed momentum. We needed to have a milestone that we were working towards. We could have just kept building it quiet for a long time more, but it was very demotivating. So that was a very big part of this. So there was a desire holistically to get out of stealth. But we didn't want to do it until we knew it'd at least be successful. But that was a key thing for me. I was working on that messaging, positioning that I was telling you, like we would have this. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]I still have the doc actually where I was like, projected on the screen and Dylan and Sean and I picked apart every word of it and sharing with a link and multiplayer is the biggest thing. That's the core differentiator. It's really funny. I remember Ivan from Notion's early days, he stopped by and was chatting, and he's like, "Wait, you can't launch with that multiplayer." And I was like, "I know." So I was like, everybody was like, that was the core thing. (00:20:36): But the idea was that we wanted to get out of stealth. We talked to Evan, our CTO, and knew it would take about another year for him to build it. And for me it was like, "Well, is there enough here to get people excited to start and to get users, get more feedback?" Because Evan was kind of building multiplayer. I don't know enough about the engineering if he was doing it on his own or not, but he was the key person doing it. But there are a lot of other things too that were being built or could be built through that year. And we wanted to get more feedback from people and to start really get started. (00:21:05): And so to me, the things that I wanted to see before just deciding like, "Okay, so we don't have our key feature. Can we still launch, or is there enough fear for people to get excited?" At least my first three months, especially before we get going for the launch with the product, and probably even after that, I would just go around with Dylan and pilot or demo Figma to companies. That was a lot of what we did. So we'd go to these companies and we'd show them Figma and we'd get their feedback, and I would be driving around in Palo Alto, around the city doing that with Dylan. And sometimes people didn't care. They were just like, "What is this? I don't want to design online," things like that. (00:21:47): But what we wanted to see, what I wanted to see was that designers were excited when they saw the tool. And once we got enough features, and I saw this pretty quickly actually when I joined Figma, is that the people that we showed it to were really interested in it and cared about it. And I remember after Vector Networks came out, after some of our other core features, there were enough things where people, I remember, they would take the laptop out of Dylan's hands when he would start showing it because they wanted to play with it. And to me, when I started seeing designers do that, even if I wasn't sure if they'd use it as a team, even if I wasn't sure if they'd buy it, we weren't selling it yet. They wanted to try it and they were excited about it. (00:22:28): And that kind of emotion, no reaction of wanting to play with it in these demos was really what gave me confidence that we were ready to launch. And we had a couple teams, small numbers, and happened to talk about metrics and how hard it is to deal with metrics of this size, but very small numbers. But we had teams who were using it full-time. So we knew that some people were using it full-time and people who weren't were really excited to try and were very impressed with the technical feat of it all and interested. And to me that was enough confidence that like, "Okay, it's worth it. Let's get out of stealth."
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这是几件事。所以我觉得首先是这个团队自己在隔离状态下默默建设了三年。这很难。我认为，摆脱隐身状态的决定的一个非常现实的部分是人们已经建造了很长时间。我们需要动力。我们需要有一个我们正在努力实现的里程碑。我们本来可以让它安静地建造更长时间，但这非常令人沮丧。所以这是其中非常重要的一部分。因此，人们整体上渴望摆脱隐身状态。但我们不想这样做，直到我们知道它至少会成功。但这对我来说是一件关键的事情。我正在研究我告诉你的信息和定位，就像我们会有这个一样。 [NEW_PARAGRAPH]我仍然保留着我以前喜欢的文档，投影在屏幕上，迪伦和肖恩和我把它的每一个字拆开，并通过链接和多人共享来共享是最重要的事情。这是核心差异化因素。真的很有趣。我记得 Notion 早期的 Ivan，他过来聊天，他说，“等等，你不能启动多人游戏。”我当时想，“我知道。”所以我想，每个人都想，这就是核心。 (00:20:36)：但我们的想法是要摆脱隐身状态。我们与我们的首席技术官埃文（Evan）进行了交谈，并知道他还需要大约一年的时间来构建它。对我来说，这就像，“好吧，这里是否有足够的东西让人们兴奋地开始并吸引用户，获得更多反馈？”因为埃文正在开发多人游戏。我不太了解工程是否是他自己做的，但他是做这件事的关键人物。但那一年还有很多其他正在建造或可能建造的东西。我们希望从人们那里获得更多反馈，并开始真正开始。 (00:21:05)：对我来说，在决定之前我想看到的事情是，“好吧，所以我们没有我们的关键功能。我们还能发布吗？或者是否有足够的恐惧让人们兴奋？”至少在我的前三个月，特别是在我们开始发布产品之前，甚至可能在那之后，我只会和 Dylan 一起向公司进行试点或演示 Figma。这就是我们所做的很多事情。所以我们会去这些公司，向他们展示Figma，然后得到他们的反馈，然后我会开车在帕洛阿尔托，在城市里和迪伦一起做这件事。有时人们并不关心。他们只是说，“这是什么？我不想在线设计”之类的事情。 (00:21:47)：但我们想看到的是，我想看到的是设计师在看到这个工具时感到兴奋。一旦我们获得了足够的功能，当我加入 Figma 时，我很快就看到了这一点，我们向其展示的人们真的对它感兴趣并关心它。我记得在 Vector Networks 推出后，在我们的其他一些核心功能之后，我记得，当迪伦开始展示笔记本电脑时，人们会从他手中夺走笔记本电脑，因为他们想玩它。对我来说，当我开始看到设计师这样做时，即使我不确定他们是否会作为一个团队使用它，即使我不确定他们是否会购买它，我们还没有出售它。他们想尝试一下，并且对此感到兴奋。 (00:22:28)：正是这种情感，没有想要在这些演示中使用它的反应，真正让我相信我们已经准备好发布。我们有几个团队，人数很少，并且碰巧谈论了指标以及处理这种规模但数量很少的指标有多么困难。但我们有团队全职使用它。所以我们知道有些人正在全职使用它，而那些没有全职使用它的人则非常兴奋地尝试，并对它的技术壮举印象深刻并且很感兴趣。对我来说，这是足够的信心，就像，“好吧，这是值得的。让我们摆脱隐身吧。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That story of the- PART 1 OF 4 ENDS [00:23:04]
turns.zh: 那个故事 - 第 1 部分（共 4 部分）结束 [00:23:04]

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: ... let's get out of stealth.
turns.zh: ...让我们摆脱隐身状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That story of the potential customer pulling the laptop from Dylan is such a good metaphor for product market fit, which people describe as you feel pull. Someone's literally pulling it from your hands. You talked about metrics that you maybe could share. What could you share there?
turns.zh: 潜在客户从迪伦那里拉走笔记本电脑的故事是产品市场契合度的一个很好的比喻，人们将其描述为你感觉拉动。有人真的把它从你手中夺走了。您谈到了您也许可以分享的指标。你能在那里分享什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: At these early days, especially with bottoms-up and with all these things... And people ask me all the time, "How do you measure things in an early stage situation?" And I maybe have a controversial point of view here. I don't think you can, from a metrics side. Your numbers are so small. One of the quotes I always like to say, and I say this now too, when we're doing stuff, because we're launching new products [inaudible 00:23:40] and it comes up a lot, is you can't optimize your way to product market fit. I don't care at the early stages if something's optimized by 5% from an email. (00:23:50): That doesn't fundamentally tell me if something's working or not, so I think metrics are really hard and signal is actually way more important. Can you get a couple people who love it, not a slight improvement of a conversion of a landing page. And so I think that metrics are really hard in that way. They can help you, but when the numbers are so small, you have to, again, trust yourself a lot more and have more intuition, but then also find more signal of the things that are working, whether it's anecdotal, talking to people, examples, and that becomes much more useful than hard metrics are sometimes.
turns.zh: 在早期，尤其是自下而上和所有这些事情......人们总是问我，“你如何在早期阶段的情况下衡量事情？”我在这里可能有一个有争议的观点。从指标方面来看，我认为你不能。你的数字这么小。我总是喜欢说的一句话，我现在也这么说，当我们在做事情时，因为我们正在推出新产品 [听不清 00:23:40] 并且它出现了很多，那就是你无法优化产品市场契合的方式。在早期阶段，我并不关心某些内容是否通过电子邮件优化了 5%。 (00:23:50)：这并不能从根本上告诉我某些东西是否有效，所以我认为指标真的很难，信号实际上更重要。你能得到几个喜欢它的人，而不是登陆页面转换的轻微改进吗？所以我认为衡量指标在这方面确实很难。它们可以帮助你，但当数字如此之小时，你必须再次更加相信自己，拥有更多的直觉，但同时也要找到更多正在发挥作用的信号，无论是轶事、与人交谈、例子，有时这比硬性指标更有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm working on a post around product market fit and a step-by-step somewhat of our guide to help people down this path. The way you described it is the way I'm thinking about it, is step one, get one company to use your product.
turns.zh: 我正在写一篇关于产品市场契合度的文章，以及一份逐步的指南，以帮助人们走上这条路。你所描述的方式就是我的想法，第一步是让一家公司使用你的产品。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Step two-
turns.zh: 第二步-

turns.en: What do they want? That was step one, and then that's not easy. That's not easy.
turns.zh: 他们想要什么？这是第一步，然后就不容易了。这并不容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. And then it's like, get them to continue using your product.
turns.zh: 正确的。然后就像是让他们继续使用你的产品。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then it's get two companies to use your product.
turns.zh: 然后就有两家公司使用你的产品。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then get someone to pay for your product. Yeah, so there's all these major milestones. Along those same lines, I saw an interview with Dylan talking about product market fit, and he had this interesting quote about how he realized first that they had product market fit a year later, which is when Microsoft, I think, was like, "Take our money. We want to pay for Figma." And he's like, "Okay, maybe this is going to work." Does that sound about right?
turns.zh: 然后让某人为您的产品付款。是的，所以有所有这些重要的里程碑。沿着同样的思路，我看到 Dylan 的一次采访谈到了产品市场契合度，他引用了一段有趣的话，讲述了他如何在一年后首次意识到他们的产品市场契合度，我认为当时微软的反应是，“拿走我们的钱。我们想为 Figma 买单。”他说：“好吧，也许这会起作用。”听起来对吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Well, it's interesting, and that goes up to the bottoms-up model that we could talk about. I think the difference, if you think about a company like Microsoft and what this looks like, this is just a really good example of this bottoms-up motion in market. Here's a funny story that I want to add. Our first meeting with Microsoft actually came, and this is the scrappiness of working in an early stage startup, because I slid into the DMs of my friend's ex-boyfriend. That's how we got our first meeting with Microsoft.
turns.zh: 嗯，这很有趣，这涉及到我们可以讨论的自下而上的模型。我认为区别在于，如果你考虑像微软这样的公司及其外观，这只是市场自下而上运动的一个很好的例子。这是我想添加的一个有趣的故事。我们与微软的第一次会面确实到来了，这就是在早期初创公司工作的斗志，因为我陷入了我朋友前男友的私信中。这就是我们与微软的第一次会面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well done.
turns.zh: 干得好。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: I know, I know. I saw that they had signed up for Figma, and I was like, "Wait a minute. I think I know this person." And that's how we chatted with them and first got feedback from them, so that's just a funny anecdote.
turns.zh: 我知道，我知道。我看到他们已经注册了 Figma，我就想，“等一下。我想我认识这个人。”这就是我们与他们聊天并首先得到他们反馈的方式，所以这只是一个有趣的轶事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This could be a new strategy if everyone's going to try to-
turns.zh: 如果每个人都尝试——

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: You literally do whatever. Uber driver, shared Lyfts, we can talk more about that. But yeah, you got to do whatever you can to get early people to try your product out and get really scrappy. But for Microsoft, over time, we would have, I think it was... What was the team that got acquired that we went into Microsoft? I'll have to remember the name, but it was a small team within Microsoft and they were... Xamarin, it was Xamarin. They were to ones who were using Figma first, and we saw that, so they were that patient zero at Microsoft. And then we had, slowly over time, more pockets within Microsoft using the tool. (00:26:28): But again, we've never gone through Microsoft procurement, Microsoft security. It just started popping up throughout the organization. And we have these really cool Node graphs that show this too, where you'd have these little pockets of people and then it would jump to another, like they'd have one more collaborator and then jump from another pocket. There were these really cool maps of how that spread within the organization. And eventually, we got to the point where that was a very comprehensive Node graph that had this massive thing of all of these people from Microsoft using the product. (00:26:55): But still, it was only on credit cards. I don't think we even had an enterprise product at this point, and so there was no salesperson for them to talk to. And Microsoft was like, "Wait a minute. We need to organize this. We need security. We need account management. We need procurement involved." And I think that that's what it was. They wanted to pay for it and they wanted us to have this enterprise product, because they had these requirements and they wanted to have a better control over it, because it was just popping up within the organization without their control. And so that's probably a good example of what that looked like as this bottoms in motion just spread to a really large organization.
turns.zh: 你确实可以做任何事。 Uber 司机、共享 Lyfts，我们可以更多地讨论这些。但是，是的，你必须尽一切努力让早期的人们尝试你的产品，并变得非常斗志旺盛。但对于微软来说，随着时间的推移，我们会，我认为是......我们进入微软时被收购的团队是什么？我必须记住这个名字，但那是 Microsoft 内部的一个小团队，他们是……Xamarin，就是 Xamarin。他们是那些首先使用 Figma 的人，我们看到了这一点，所以他们是微软的零号病人。然后，随着时间的推移，我们慢慢地在微软内部有了更多的人使用这个工具。 (00:26:28)：但同样，我们从未经历过微软采购、微软安全。它刚刚开始在整个组织中出现。我们有这些非常酷的节点图也显示了这一点，你会有这些小口袋里的人，然后它会跳到另一个口袋里，就像他们会有一个更多的合作者，然后从另一个口袋里跳出来。这些非常酷的地图展示了它如何在组织内传播。最终，我们得到了一个非常全面的节点图，其中包含来自 Microsoft 的所有使用该产品的人员的大量信息。 (00:26:55)：但仍然仅限于信用卡。我认为我们此时甚至还没有企业产品，因此没有销售人员可供他们交谈。微软的反应是，“等一下。我们需要组织起来。我们需要安全。我们需要帐户管理。我们需要参与采购。”我认为事情就是这样。他们想要为此付费，他们希望我们拥有这个企业产品，因为他们有这些要求，他们希望对其有更好的控制，因为它只是在组织内突然出现而不受他们的控制。因此，这可能是一个很好的例子，说明这种底部运动刚刚蔓延到一个非常大的组织。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This Node graph thing, is that a tool you built that's showing, helping you visualize within a company how it's all clustering? Or what is that?
turns.zh: 这个节点图是您构建的一个工具，可以帮助您可视化公司内部的所有集群情况？或者那是什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Well, our data science team built it. I don't know if it's like... Yes, I'm sure it's an internal tool. You type in the name of an organization and it just pulls up everybody. And it shows, because Figma spreads through new users, but also gen one, gen two, these people invite people. And you can see these Node graphs of how somebody started Figma, maybe at the center, and then they invited someone else, and then it shows how that spread. (00:28:16): And so you get these clusters, and you can see the clusters are teams, but then you can see someone invited someone in a different org to a file and then that started a new center of a cluster. They're really interesting. And you can pull up, you can type in any org, any org at Figma and see what that Node graph looks like. But they're super interesting to see how those spread.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们的数据科学团队构建了它。我不知道它是否像...是的，我确定它是一个内部工具。我只记得 Node 中有一个网站或者我们会使用的东西，你可以在组织名称中输入它。你仍然可以做到这一点。它位于我们的数据分析系统内。你输入一个组织的名称，它就会拉出每个人。它表明，由于 Figma 通过新用户传播，而且还通过第一代、第二代用户传播，这些人邀请了人们。你可以看到这些节点图，显示有人如何启动Figma，也许是在中心，然后他们邀请了其他人，然后它显示了它是如何传播的。 (00:28:16)：所以你得到了这些集群，你可以看到集群是团队，但是你可以看到有人邀请不同组织中的某人加入文件，然后启动了一个新的集群中心。他们真的很有趣。你可以拉起，你可以在 Figma 上输入任何组织，任何组织，看看节点图是什么样的。但他们非常有趣地看到这些是如何传播的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. And I imagine that also informs how you go to market by figuring out who spreads to who and who's often [inaudible 00:28:45].
turns.zh: 那太酷了。我想这也可以告诉你如何通过弄清楚谁传播给谁以及谁经常传播[听不清00:28:45]来进入市场。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Totally, and that's when these internal champions, that's what the key is. And that's maybe the takeaway of how important these internal champions are, because you just need someone to land there and then them maybe passing it up. You could hover over and see this person's at the center of this Node graph and all of these people that spread from this one person at the company. And that, I think, was the unlock to be like, "Oh yeah, these internal champions, they're really the key to all of this."
turns.zh: 完全地，这就是这些内部冠军的时候，这就是关键。这也许就是这些内部冠军的重要性，因为你只需要有人登陆那里，然后他们可能会放弃它。您可以将鼠标悬停在该节点图的中心，并看到此人位于该节点图的中心，以及公司中从该人传播的所有这些人。我认为，这就是“哦，是的，这些内部冠军，他们确实是这一切的关键”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember it spreading at Airbnb early on. I think Airbnb was one of the early customers and it was just one designer, a few designers starting to spread to the product managers. I was just a member on the team being like, "Goddamn it, we just switched to Sketch. Are we going to switch again to a new product?"
turns.zh: 我记得它很早就在 Airbnb 传播开来。我认为 Airbnb 是早期的客户之一，它只是一位设计师，几位设计师开始扩展到产品经理。我只是团队中的一员，“天哪，我们刚刚切换到 Sketch。我们要再次切换到新产品吗？”

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: That was the hardest thing to feel like I don't want to switch twice. That was definitely something we had to get over.
turns.zh: 这是最难的事情，让我觉得我不想换两次。这绝对是我们必须克服的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it happened for good reasons. Okay, one last thing that you mentioned that I wanted to follow up on. You said something about shared Lyfts, and maybe that's a funny story of some sort.
turns.zh: 但这是有充分理由的。好的，你提到的我想跟进的最后一件事。你谈到了共享 Lyfts 的事情，也许这是一个有趣的故事。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Oh, I don't know specifically. Actually, Dylan specifically is such a hustler, especially in those early days. And he would just, really anyone that he would meet, he would talk about Figma with them. I don't remember who it was, but there was definitely a situation where he met someone in a Lyft and then they became one of our users. He used every angle he could to try to get introduced to new designers, especially in his pre-launch days where we didn't have as many connections to just get people to try it out and get more feedback.
turns.zh: 哦，具体我也不清楚。事实上，迪伦就是这样一个骗子，尤其是在早期。他会与任何他遇到的人谈论Figma。我不记得是谁了，但肯定有一种情况，他在 Lyft 上遇到了某人，然后他们就成为了我们的用户之一。他利用一切可能的角度来尝试向新设计师介绍，特别是在他发布前的日子里，我们没有那么多的联系来让人们尝试并获得更多反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Let's get back on track. We were talking about the go-to-market motion that you executed and modeled at Figma. There's two steps, right? Step one is get ICs to love you, and then step two is help it spread from that person, right?
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。让我们回到正轨吧。我们正在讨论您在 Figma 执行和建模的上市动议。有两步，对吧？第一步是让 IC 爱你，然后第二步是帮助它从那个人那里传播，对吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yep, yep.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So, let's start with step one.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。那么，让我们从第一步开始。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like I said, obviously, it'd be awesome if somebody loved your product at a company. What did you actually do to make that happen in the early days?
turns.zh: 就像我说的，显然，如果公司里有人喜欢你的产品，那就太棒了。为了实现这一目标，您早期实际上做了什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah. It's really interesting when you think about the early days too, because you're like, "All right. We don't exist." How do you get them to love you when literally, they've never heard of you before? Also, like you were saying, in your situation, "Oh, I used Sketch. I was maybe in Photoshop before that, something else. I just made the switch over to this new tool. We finally got it working. I really don't want to move tools again." You have that inherent thing against it there. Especially I thought about this, and I think there are four main areas that we focused on to make this start, to get it going, and then we kind of still do this stuff today. (00:31:05): The first thing is all about credibility. I think in the early days especially, credibility is so important in establishing that initial credibility, again, especially with a technical audience like designers. The second is actually building the product with your users. And I know you had Sho on your podcast and he talked a lot about this too, just the customer obsession that we have the care of, especially that editor tool. (00:31:28): The third is finding a place where you can, in a way, that you can build this relationship over time. Maybe that's specifically through a channel where they don't have to come to you, because they don't really care about you yet and they're probably not going to convert right away or start using you right away, so how do you get them to stick with you over time? So, find out the channel where you can do that and then continue to build that relationship with them. And then the four is just being extremely transparent and honest to build that relationship with people. I know those all sound really fuzzy, so maybe we can go into them specifically.
turns.zh: 是的。当你回想早期的时候，这真的很有趣，因为你会想，“好吧。我们不存在。”当他们以前从未听说过你时，你如何让他们爱你？另外，正如您所说，在您的情况下，“哦，我使用 Sketch。在那之前我可能使用过 Photoshop，或者其他东西。我刚刚切换到这个新工具。我们终于让它工作了。我真的不想再移动工具了。”你有固有的反对它的东西。我特别想到了这一点，我认为我们重点关注四个主要领域来启动这个项目，让它继续下去，然后我们今天仍然在做这些事情。 (00:31:05)：首先是可信度。我认为，尤其是在早期，可信度对于建立最初的可信度非常重要，尤其是对于设计师等技术受众而言。第二个是实际与用户一起构建产品。我知道你的播客上有 Sho，他也谈到了很多关于这一点，只是我们所关心的客户痴迷，尤其是那个编辑器工具。 (00:31:28)：第三是找到一个地方，在某种程度上，你可以随着时间的推移建立这种关系。也许这是专门通过一个他们不必来找你的渠道，因为他们还没有真正关心你，他们可能不会立即转换或开始使用你，那么你如何让他们随着时间的推移坚持与你在一起呢？因此，找到可以做到这一点的渠道，然后继续与他们建立关系。然后，这四个人就以极其透明和诚实的方式与人们建立这种关系。我知道这些听起来都很模糊，所以也许我们可以具体讨论一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. I was going to ask.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我正想问。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Because they sound really fuzzy when you talk about them. A lot of this stuff is hard like that, where you're like, "Oh, that just sounds like buzzwords." I can give you some examples of these four things, so maybe it helps to give some color to it.
turns.zh: 因为当你谈论它们时，它们听起来真的很模糊。很多这样的东西都很难，你会想，“哦，这听起来就像流行语。”我可以给你举一些关于这四件事的例子，所以也许它有助于给它一些色彩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 伟大的。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Let's start with the first one, credibility. Okay. I was the first marketer at Figma. I think one of the things I learned right away, very quickly was that designers don't want to hear from marketers. They don't want to be marketed to and they have an extremely high bullshit meter. You use a word like efficiency, collaboration, all of those buzzwords, and they're just like, "I don't want to hear this." Traditional product marketing kind of stuff just doesn't work. They wanted to hear technical features. They wanted to understand how technical features work. They want to hear, "How am I going to use this?" And then they'll see the benefits, but they don't want to hear from marketers and they don't want to be marketed to. (00:32:55): And so I think especially with our audience in the early days, one of the things that I did was really try to not market. And that's so funny as a marketer to say that, but that was really core to build authenticity with people. And so the way that we did that in the early days was what we had was the tool, and that's pretty much what we had, and we had a design team and we had an engineering team. We did some cool stuff in the tool. First of all, the tool itself was a technical feat. It was the first time it used video game technology, WebGL. Evan's a prodigy. The fact that he got a design tool to work on the internet was just amazing, and so there was a lot of engineering interest there, credibility building of, "How did you get this to work?" [NEW_PARAGRAPH]I got him to make technical content and that, I think, went to number one on Hacker News, that people were just interested in him. And then we had a design team, and our design team was our target audience. And so we talked a lot about how we chose to build features, all the things that went into it. And so many of the primitives of design tools have been like that forever, and so we changed the stuff. One of them would be how we did grids or how we did vector networks, and we'd go into these really deep details of how we chose to make those product decisions, all the craft decisions that went into it. (00:34:08): I remember one of my bars were deciding if something would hit this or not, if they would be interested was, "Did I understand it?" You know what I mean? And if I understood it, it was probably too basic, or if I could have written it myself, it was probably too basic. I remember we did one on grids in the early days, and we went really deep on Joseph Muller Brockmann and his influence on grids. And now, I very much know who Joseph Muller Brockmann is because I work with designers, but at the time, I had to Google it. I was like, "Who is this?" But that was one of my bars for if something would be good enough for our technical content, was if I could have written it, it's not good enough. And so that was key for us in building credibility, because we had this design team. (00:34:47): And then when six months after we launched, I actually got to hire someone to do marketing with me, the first person I hired was actually a designer advocate. So it was not a marketer, it was someone who was a designer. The designers and the engineers that I was trying to get to help me with stuff also had to design and build the product, so they didn't have a ton of time. But this designer advocate was working full-time with me on this stuff, and he came from our user base. He was one of the very few people in the early days who just loved the product and was very passionate about it. And that became his full-time job was to represent, to meet with users, talk to them, to write content and create content, and to bring that back to the product, and that was what he did. (00:35:32): And that designer advocacy positions actually scaled with Figma, and we still have it today. It's extreme. I think it's the magic dust, we call it, that we sprinkle on go-to-market to make a lot of our go-to-market function work. But yeah, we didn't focus on marketing, or traditional marketing. We're very focused on the technical aspects.
turns.zh: 让我们从第一个开始，可信度。好的。我是 Figma 的第一位营销人员。我认为我很快就学到的一件事是设计师不想听到营销人员的意见。他们不想被推销，而且他们的废话量表非常高。你使用像效率、协作这样的词，所有这些流行词，他们就像是，“我不想听这个。”传统的产品营销之类的东西根本行不通。他们想听听技术特点。他们想了解技术功能是如何工作的。他们想听到“我将如何使用这个？”然后他们会看到好处，但他们不想听到营销人员的意见，也不想被推销。 (00:32:55)：所以我认为，尤其是对于早期的观众，我所做的事情之一就是尝试不营销。作为一名营销人员，这样说很有趣，但这确实是与人们建立真实性的核心。因此，我们早期的做法就是我们所拥有的工具，这几乎就是我们所拥有的，我们有一个设计团队，我们有一个工程团队。我们在该工具中做了一些很酷的事情。首先，该工具本身就是一项技术壮举。这是它第一次使用视频游戏技术 WebGL。埃文是个神童。事实上，他得到了一个可以在互联网上运行的设计工具，这真是太棒了，所以人们对工程产生了很大的兴趣，建立了可信度，“你是如何让它发挥作用的？” [NEW_PARAGRAPH]我让他制作技术内容，我认为这在黑客新闻上排名第一，人们只是对他感兴趣。然后我们有一个设计团队，我们的设计团队就是我们的目标受众。因此，我们讨论了很多关于如何选择构建功能以及其中涉及的所有内容。设计工具的许多原语一直都是这样，所以我们改变了这些东西。其中之一是我们如何制作网格或如何制作矢量网络，我们将深入探讨我们如何选择做出这些产品决策的真正深入的细节，以及其中涉及的所有工艺决策。 (00:34:08)：我记得我的一个酒吧正在决定是否有东西会击中这个，如果他们感兴趣的话，“我理解了吗？”你知道我的意思？如果我理解它，它可能太基础了，或者如果我可以自己写它，它可能太基础了。我记得我们早期在网格上做了一个，我们非常深入地研究了约瑟夫·穆勒·布罗克曼（Joseph Muller Brockmann）和他对网格的影响。现在，我非常知道约瑟夫·穆勒·布罗克曼是谁，因为我与设计师一起工作，但当时，我不得不用谷歌搜索它。我当时想，“这是谁？”但这是我的障碍之一，因为如果某些东西对于我们的技术内容来说足够好，那就是如果我可以写它，它还不够好。因此，这对我们建立信誉至关重要，因为我们有这个设计团队。 (00:34:47)：当我们推出六个月后，我实际上必须聘请一个人和我一起进行营销，我聘请的第一个人实际上是一位设计师倡导者。所以这不是一个营销人员，而是一个设计师。我试图帮助我解决问题的设计师和工程师也必须设计和构建产品，所以他们没有太多的时间。但这位设计师倡导者正在与我全职合作做这件事，他来自我们的用户群。他是早期极少数热爱该产品并对它充满热情的人之一。他的全职工作就是代表、会见用户、与他们交谈、编写内容和创建内容，并将其带回到产品中，这就是他所做的。 (00:35:32)：设计师的倡导职位实际上与 Figma 一起扩展，我们今天仍然拥有它。这是极端的。我认为这就是我们所说的“魔法灰尘”，我们撒在“上市”上，使我们的许多“上市”功能发挥作用。但是，是的，我们并没有专注于营销或传统营销。我们非常关注技术方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many little lessons there. The designer advocate hire reminds me of something that Datadog did, where they hired engineers to write their blog posts.
turns.zh: 那里有很多小教训。聘请设计师倡导者让我想起了 Datadog 所做的事情，他们聘请工程师来撰写博客文章。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: That's a great idea. Yes, exactly what we did. Yes.
turns.zh: 这是个好主意。是的，正是我们所做的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, ways you build credibility, just kind of mirroring back what you just shared, one is writing content. Basically, putting out blog posts that designers would be like, "Oh, wow. This is really interesting," and start to feel like, "Oh, Figma keeps coming up in these really interesting pieces of content."
turns.zh: 因此，建立可信度的方法，只是反映你刚刚分享的内容，其中之一就是编写内容。基本上，发布博客文章时，设计师会说，“哦，哇。这真的很有趣”，然后开始感觉，“哦，Figma 不断出现在这些非常有趣的内容中。”

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, even if they were using it, and I think that that was important. When we launched, people wanted to test it because it was cool and see what it is, but then they bounced. They're like, "All right. This isn't advanced enough. I'll come back later." Which is why we're give them reasons to come back, being like, "Oh, yeah, but the pen tools always worked like this, but we did it like that. You should test that out." And so we kept giving them these nuggets of reasons to come back in. Remember, this was also before multiplayer, and so we couldn't collaborate, so it was use the tools to do these things. That really helps people come back into the tool and spend a little bit more time in it.
turns.zh: 是的，即使他们正在使用它，我认为这很重要。当我们推出时，人们想测试它，因为它很酷，看看它是什么，但后来他们就反弹了。他们会说，“好吧。这还不够先进。我稍后再回来。”这就是为什么我们给他们回来的理由，就像，“哦，是的，但是钢笔工具总是这样工作，但我们是这样做的。你应该测试一下。”所以我们不断地给他们提供回来的理由。请记住，这也是在多人游戏之前，所以我们无法协作，所以只能使用工具来完成这些事情。这确实可以帮助人们重新使用该工具并花更多时间在其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many posts would you say you put out in that first six months, just to give people a sense of here's how much? It's probably not a ton, right? It's probably some few really good ones.
turns.zh: 您会说您在前六个月内发布了多少帖子，只是为了让人们了解这里有多少？可能不是很多，对吧？这可能是一些非常好的。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: They took a long time. Also, I had to work with an engineer or a designer to do every single one. Maybe 10 at most. But those ones that went out, we tried to get on Hacker News. We tried to get on Designer News at the time. Twitter, we can jump into that, but it was also extremely big for us. And so it was more about quality than it was about quantity.
turns.zh: 他们花了很长时间。此外，我必须与工程师或设计师合作来完成每一项工作。也许最多 10 个。但那些出去的，我们试图上《黑客新闻》。当时我们试图收听《设计师新闻》。 Twitter，我们可以跳进去，但它对我们来说也非常大。因此，质量比数量更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so one is put out great content. People are like, "Oh, wow. Figma's got some new ideas and maybe I should pay attention." The other is having someone that's that function actually talk to them.
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的，这样就发布了很棒的内容。人们会说，“哦，哇。Figma 有一些新想法，也许我应该关注。”另一个是让具有该功能的人真正与他们交谈。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yes. That was when we started accelerating this much, much more is when we brought in that designer advocate to help us with this full-time.
turns.zh: 是的。就在那时，我们开始加快步伐，更多的是当我们聘请设计师倡导者全职帮助我们完成这项工作时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Okay. Let's move to the next one, which I think is building with your customers.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。好的。让我们进入下一个，我认为这是与您的客户一起构建的。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: That one, I know you talked to Show, he talked a lot about this, this idea of customer obsession and of building with your customers. And it also goes back to that whole decision that we talked about earlier, about when to come out of stealth. You can only build so much with your customers when you're in stealth, because you don't have that many that know about you. But especially, even in the early days when we only had a couple people, we really did listen. And back to also what you were saying earlier about those steps to product market fit, get one person to use it. That's really what we were focused on, especially in the very, very early days. (00:38:10): I remember the first one, I think I've told this story before, but was that we had Coda. They were our first user and they were based in Palo Alto. Dylan and I drove down and demoed the product to them, and they were the first ones. Their designer, Jeremy, was like, "Yes, we'll take this on full-time." And I remember, we were both like, "What? Really? You will?" That was the first person who said yes to us, and so we were so excited. This was a huge milestone. We went to Oren's Hummus in Palo Alto on the way back to the office to bring some back for the team to celebrate. We were just so stoked. (00:38:41): And then we got back to the office, and I think Dylan gets a text from Jeremy being like, "Oh, yeah. I tried to share this with Philippe, my engineer, and he can't get the file to open, so I guess he can't use it." And we're like, "What is it? What happened? We finally got someone." And I remember Dylan was like, "Everybody drop everything. We have to fix this." And after some looking at the servers and things, they were like, "Nothing's wrong," and then they realized it was a problem with Philippe's MacBook. Evan [inaudible 00:39:08] had a car, so Dylan had to drive Evan down to Palo Alto to fix the MacBook of Philippe just to get them to use the product. So anyway, get them to stick around. That's the first one. (00:39:17): But the building with people, the way that we did that was largely through just each person. We really cared and listened to their feedback, especially when there were only a few people. One way we did that was, I remember we implemented Intercom back in the early days, and there were so few users and so few of us that everybody was on Intercom all day too. And so we'd get a chat and I would jump in sometimes. Dylan would jump in, an engineer would jump in. And he'd open up a chat with people and they'd actually debug the product with us live. They'd be like, "I have this bug," and this engineer would be like, "Let me QA it right now." And so that was one example. We all did support back in that day, and the engineers would talk to users directly, get their feedback, and then go immediately fix things like bugs. (00:40:02): And so those are just examples of in the early days, what that looks like, and that just scales a lot over time as you're growing and you're talking to more people. That advocate ended up helping us a ton when they came on board, because some of this stuff, I mean, none of this stuff scales. Your engineers can't do support forever. In the early days, that becomes really important. But when we brought that advocate in, their whole job was talking to users, getting them to try to use the product, but then taking their feedback back when it wasn't something that wasn't working. (00:40:34): That helped us scale a lot, so that became really essential, and then telling people, "Oh, we fixed this." It made them feel more ownership of the tool too, being like, "Oh, yeah. I asked them to do this. They did it." That's just another way where you just build a strong relationship with people, because they feel very invested in your journey with you.
turns.zh: 我知道你和 Show 谈过，他谈了很多关于客户至上以及与客户共建的想法。这也可以追溯到我们之前讨论过的整个决定，即何时退出隐身状态。当你秘密行动时，你只能与你的客户建立这么多的东西，因为你没有那么多人了解你。但尤其是，即使在早期我们只有几个人的时候，我们也确实在倾听。回到您之前所说的关于产品市场契合度的步骤，让一个人使用它。这确实是我们关注的重点，尤其是在非常非常早期的时候。 (00:38:10)：我记得第一个，我想我以前讲过这个故事，但我们有 Coda。他们是我们的第一个用户，他们的总部位于帕洛阿尔托。迪伦和我开车过来向他们演示产品，他们是第一批。他们的设计师 Jeremy 说：“是的，我们会全职承担这个工作。”我记得，我们都说，“什么？真的吗？你会的吗？”那是第一个对我们说“是”的人，所以我们非常兴奋。这是一个巨大的里程碑。在返回办公室的路上，我们去了帕洛阿尔托的奥伦鹰嘴豆泥，带了一些回来供团队庆祝。我们太兴奋了。 (00:38:41)：然后我们回到办公室，我想迪伦收到了杰里米发来的一条短信，内容是：“哦，是的。我试图与我的工程师菲利普分享这个，但他无法打开该文件，所以我猜他无法使用它。”我们会说，“这是什么？发生了什么事？我们终于找到人了。”我记得迪伦说，“每个人都放弃一切。我们必须解决这个问题。”在检查了服务器和其他东西之后，他们说“没有什么问题”，然后他们意识到这是 Philippe 的 MacBook 的问题。 Evan [听不清 00:39:08] 有辆车，所以 Dylan 不得不开车送 Evan 去帕洛阿尔托修理 Philippe 的 MacBook，只是为了让他们使用该产品。所以无论如何，让他们留下来。这是第一个。 (00:39:17)：但是这座由人组成的建筑，我们所做的方式很大程度上是通过每个人。我们非常关心并听取了他们的反馈，尤其是在只有少数人的情况下。我们这样做的一种方法是，我记得我们在早期就实现了 Intercom，当时用户很少，我们的人也很少，所以每个人也整天都在使用 Intercom。所以我们会聊天，有时我也会插话。迪伦会介入，工程师也会介入。他会与人们聊天，他们会与我们一起现场调试产品。他们会说，“我有这个错误”，而这位工程师会说，“让我现在就对其进行质量检查。”这就是一个例子。那天我们都做了支持，工程师会直接与用户交谈，获取他们的反馈，然后立即修复错误等问题。 (00:40:02)：所以这些只是早期的例子，随着时间的推移，随着你的成长和与更多人交谈，它会扩大很多。当这位倡导者加入时，他们最终为我们提供了很多帮助，因为其中一些东西，我的意思是，这些东西都没有规模。您的工程师无法永远提供支持。在早期，这变得非常重要。但是当我们引入该倡导者时，他们的全部工作就是与用户交谈，让他们尝试使用该产品，然后在产品没有出现问题时收回他们的反馈。 (00:40:34)：这帮助我们扩大了规模，因此这变得非常重要，然后告诉人们，“哦，我们解决了这个问题。”这也让他们对这个工具有了更多的归属感，就像，“哦，是的。我要求他们这样做。他们做到了。”这只是你与人们建立牢固关系的另一种方式，因为他们觉得你对你的旅程非常投入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which goes back to building credibility.
turns.zh: 这又回到了建立信誉的问题。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Absolutely, absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对，绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many important lessons there. You talked about scaling this, but interestingly, this is very much doing things that don't scale; driving to their office, fixing their wifi on their laptop.
turns.zh: 那里有很多重要的教训。您谈到了扩展这一点，但有趣的是，这在很大程度上是在做一些无法扩展的事情；开车去他们的办公室，在笔记本电脑上修复无线网络。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Early days, nothing scales in the early days. You just have to do it anyway.
turns.zh: 早期，早期没有任何规模。无论如何你都必须这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just as a tangent, we're talking about getting people to love your product initially. Why is love so important? That's a really high bar, and I imagine you have an interesting insight on just why it needs to be that level of appreciation.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我们谈论的是让人们一开始就喜欢你的产品。为什么爱如此重要？这是一个非常高的标准，我想你对为什么需要达到这种程度的欣赏有一个有趣的见解。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, and it doesn't have to be over time. These are all things that maybe they just use it first or they're interested, but by the time you're getting to the organization level, or I'm spreading this to my other spheres of influence, like my community, people I know, you're kind of putting yourself on the line. You're taking a risk when you're doing that, especially if it's your job. You're bringing other people in, and you're not going to do that unless you really believe in something. And so just using it isn't enough to get someone over that stage of going from just a user to a champion. But also as you're building product, you're always like, oh, well I could go do all of these fixes and bug updates, but I also have to go build new stuff to grow. And that's always a tension with any company as you're looking at a roadmap. One of the ways that we've done that and still continue to focus on things that people care about that's so related to the craft of quality is through we do quality weeks with engineering. (00:52:53): And then we decided a couple years ago, we had this idea where we were like, oh, what if we package all of those quality updates up into one thing and launch them together and we could even show the tweet or the forum request that spurred us to do this. And that was where our idea of little big updates came, which is a launch that we do every year. Figma, they come from these quality weeks with engineering, that's where the engineers can just go and look at Twitter, talk to our support team, get all these small things that annoy people to fix them, and they just fix them all and they get so many done. And then we launch them all together. And that's one of our most popular launches that we do because people are like, yes, I care about this. This improves my quality of life every single day. (00:53:37): Back to that discussion of two clicks versus one click and things like that, they're that small, but we still do it. And I love that little big updates when I think, Airbnb did something like that too, with the a hundred updates thing on their website.
turns.zh: 我认为有两个例子。一是与用户一起构建。因为我认为这是一个我喜欢参与的好领域，因为你会想，你如何扩展它？您会收到如此多的错误请求，当您访问我们论坛上的功能请求页面时，就会发现数量如此之多。但当你构建产品时，你总是会想，哦，好吧，我可以去做所有这些修复和错误更新，但我也必须去构建新的东西来成长。当你在考虑路线图时，这对任何公司来说都是一个紧张的问题。我们已经做到这一点并且仍然继续关注人们关心的与质量工艺密切相关的事情的方法之一是通过我们进行工程质量周。 (00:52:53)：几年前我们决定，我们有这样的想法，哦，如果我们将所有这些质量更新打包成一个东西并一起启动它们，我们甚至可以显示促使我们这样做的推文或论坛请求。这就是我们“小而大的更新”的想法的由来，这是我们每年都会进行的发布。 Figma，他们来自这些质量周的工程，工程师们可以去看看 Twitter，与我们的支持团队交谈，解决所有这些让人们烦恼的小问题来解决它们，他们只是解决所有这些问题，然后他们就完成了很多工作。然后我们一起启动它们。这是我们所做的最受欢迎的发布之一，因为人们会说，是的，我关心这个。这每天都提高了我的生活质量。 (00:53:37)：回到两次点击与一次点击之类的讨论，它们很小，但我们仍然这样做。当我想到 Airbnb 也做了类似的事情时，我喜欢那些小的大更新，在他们的网站上有一百个更新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Airbnb has shifted fully to that, which is only big launches, just wait twice a year and launch a bunch of stuff. That's exactly, that's fully how they operate.
turns.zh: Airbnb 已经完全转向这种方式，即只推出大型产品，每年只需等待两次，然后推出一堆东西。这就是他们的运作方式。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: That's another way that we do the building with, and I think that even giving the engineers, we give them the ability to pick them, right? So they're like, oh, yep, this tweet, I want to fix this bug.
turns.zh: 这是我们建造的另一种方式，我认为即使给了工程师，我们也让他们有能力选择他们，对吗？所以他们就像，哦，是的，这条推文，我想修复这个错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's got to be so satisfying.
turns.zh: 那一定很满足吧

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And in the marketing even, we'll pull examples like, oh yeah, that for one, the person who said that. So that one's big. And then on the transparency side, I think where this gets hard at scale is all of a sudden you have a lot of people who care about your products. And I think it's really easy as a brand because you are a brand at this point, as you're getting bigger to be like, oh, I can hide behind my handle or the Figma handle, or do I really have to say something about this? And so just two examples of things like that where you just, we've chosen to be transparent when we didn't have to be or you might not, or downtime. Downtime is always a big deal. And I remember there was a specific instance, I think it was last year, maybe two years ago, where there was this issue with these servers and an AWS cluster went down and we didn't know what was going on. (00:55:01): And so we had downtime multiple times in a week and people were pissed, right? Things were not going well. Again, back on Twitter, we built... The double-edged sword of Twitter is you build this strong communication channel with your users and they communicate right back to you if they're not happy. So it's inundating us. And I remember we did a public postmortem and we always do that. If something happens or something goes wrong, we're like, yeah, that was bad. Here's what happened and here's the technical reason and here's how we fixed it. And then we tweeted that and promoted it and took just full accountability for it. And we always choose to make those choices when they're hard. And that was just one example. But I think the hardest example, and back to your question of the most stressful days at Figma, the true most stressful day Figma, for me, was the day that we announced the acquisition. (00:55:52): That was probably one of the harder moments of my career, where... My brand is social, that's my job, is running social. And all of a sudden you have this onslaught on social and you have to figure out what to do. And I remember the way that we announced it was we just retweeted Dylan. That was all that we had said (00:56:07): Raji on our team, I remember I was talking to him about it and he was like, "We've got to talk to our users. We just have to talk to them directly. We have to show we're the same company. We just have to not hide behind the brand." And he was totally right. And so I remember we decided that day that the next day we just had to have an open public forum where we could talk directly with our users and let them ask us any questions. And so we'd held the Twitter space the next day with Dylan and Cho and Raji and Tom, and we just had it open and people could ask us anything they wanted and we were able to be just really honest and transparent with them about everything that we could. (00:56:44): And I think that that is just a really good example of how even when it's really, really, really, really hard, you still have to just be transparent. And I think that that's when the tide started to turn of people giving us a chance to prove that everything would be great, even when it's the highest stakes and the hardest thing of still listening to people, maintaining that connection and not hiding behind the brand.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。甚至在营销中，我们也会举一些例子，比如，哦，是的，就是那个说这句话的人。所以那个很大。然后在透明度方面，我认为这在规模上变得困难的是突然间有很多人关心你的产品。我认为作为一个品牌这真的很容易，因为你现在就是一个品牌，随着你变得越来越大，就像，哦，我可以躲在我的手柄或 Figma 手柄后面，或者我真的必须对此说些什么吗？这只是两个例子，比如我们选择保持透明，而我们不必这样做，或者您可能不需要，或者停机时间。停机总是一件大事。我记得有一个特定的实例，我想是去年，也许是两年前，这些服务器出现了这个问题，AWS 集群出现故障，我们不知道发生了什么。 (00:55:01)：所以我们一周内多次停机，人们很生气，对吗？事情进展不顺利。再说一次，回到 Twitter，我们建立了... Twitter 的双刃剑是你与用户建立了这个强大的沟通渠道，如果他们不满意，他们会立即与你沟通。所以它淹没了我们。我记得我们进行了公开事后分析，而且我们总是这样做。如果发生什么事或出了问题，我们会说，是的，那很糟糕。这是发生的事情，这是技术原因，这是我们修复它的方法。然后我们在推特上发布了这一消息并进行了宣传，并对此承担了全部责任。我们总是在困难的时候选择做出这些选择。这只是一个例子。但我认为最难的例子，回到你关于 Figma 压力最大的日子的问题，Figma 对我来说真正压力最大的一天是我们宣布收购的那一天。 (00:55:52)：这可能是我职业生涯中最困难的时刻之一，其中......我的品牌是社交的，这就是我的工作，就是运营社交。突然之间，你在社交上受到了冲击，你必须弄清楚该怎么做。我记得我们宣布的方式是转发迪伦的推文。这就是我们所说的全部内容 (00:56:07)：Raji 在我们团队中，我记得我正在和他谈论这件事，他说，“我们必须与我们的用户交谈。我们只需要直接与他们交谈。我们必须表明我们是同一家公司。我们只需要不要躲在品牌后面。”他是完全正确的。所以我记得那天我们决定第二天我们必须有一个开放的公共论坛，我们可以直接与我们的用户交谈，让他们问我们任何问题。因此，我们第二天与 Dylan、Cho、Raji 和 Tom 一起开设了 Twitter 空间，我们只是将其开放，人们可以问我们任何他们想要的东西，我们能够对他们诚实和透明地谈论我们所能做的一切。 (00:56:44)：我认为这只是一个很好的例子，说明即使事情真的非常非常困难，你仍然必须保持透明。我认为，从那时起，人们的潮流开始转变，让我们有机会证明一切都会很棒，即使这是最高风险和最困难的事情，仍然倾听人们的意见，保持这种联系，而不是躲在品牌后面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like transparency is core to the values of Figma. Have you codified your values and is that one of them and is there anything there?
turns.zh: 感觉透明度是 Figma 价值观的核心。您是否已将自己的价值观编入法典？这是其中之一吗？其中有什么吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Interesting. We have codified our values. It isn't explicitly listed out, which is interesting, but I think of it as our value, especially with our users. turns.zh: 有趣的。我们已经将我们的价值观编入法典。它没有明确列出，这很有趣，但我认为这是我们的价值，尤其是对我们的用户而言。我们经常思考我们的价值观，比如享受乐趣、建立社区、热爱你的手艺，所有这些肯定都会实现、发挥，但也许这应该是其中之一，因为我认为它对于我们如何做出决策以及我们决定要走哪条路的框架至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also we mentioned Cho a couple of times, but on Twitter, he is always asking people, what do you need in the editor? Here's what's going great.

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Absolutely. It's still how we get so much feedback is talking to people directly and Kris will come on when people have bugs and just respond to them. He's our CTO. People are just actively on there, listening to people, fixing bugs, responding.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我们获得如此多反馈的方式仍然是直接与人们交谈，当人们遇到错误时，克里斯就会出现并做出回应。他是我们的首席技术官。人们只是积极地在那里，倾听人们的意见，修复错误，做出回应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to shift to kind of the second step of the go-to-market motion, but before I do that, I have a couple of things I wanted to touch on briefly. I was on Twitter the days of Config, and it's just my whole feed was just like, oh my god, Config is the best thing. So many talks and so many people.
turns.zh: 我想转向上市动议的第二步，但在此之前，我想简单谈一下几件事。一是你没有提到 Config，你举办的这次会议，我认为这是一个很好的例子，可以扩展你正在谈论的很多事情。它曾经是 Twitter，社交图谱，在 Twitter 上找人。现在，这就像一场我认为人们喜欢的史诗般的会议。在 Config 出现的时候，我就在 Twitter 上，我的整个动态就是这样，天哪，Config 是最好的东西。这么多的谈话和这么多的人。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Config is such a good example. I remember, I can happily talk about Config. The way that we do Config, I think... I'd never run a conference before, maybe that's probably part of it. And I brought somebody on who had, but she and I were both sitting together and being like, okay, so we're doing a conference. How do we get the content for this conference? What do we do? And we didn't know. And so we just decided, oh, so much of what we do is listen to our users. Let's put out this call for proposals and see what they want to talk about. And so that's how we got and get a lot of our content for the conference. And a lot of it comes back to what I was talking about earlier, which is very technical deep content that targets individual contributors for the practitioners of the tool. (00:59:20): And through that process, we build these relationships with these speakers, our advocates help them shape their talks. And then I think that we do produce really strong technical content through that process and through Config. And we're also able to, with these people that we work with, help them grow their own profiles and that also helps them stay more connected to us, helps them become thought leaders in their own right. We're talking directly to how to use the tool and the things that individual contributors are still dealing with.
turns.zh: 配置就是一个很好的例子。我记得，我可以愉快地谈论Config。我认为我们进行配置的方式......我以前从未举办过会议，也许这可能是其中的一部分。我找了一个参加过会议的人来，但她和我坐在一起，说，好吧，我们正在开一个会议。我们如何获取本次会议的内容？我们该怎么办？我们不知道。所以我们决定，哦，我们所做的大部分工作就是倾听用户的意见。让我们发起征集提案，看看他们想讨论什么。这就是我们为会议获取大量内容的方式。其中很多内容都回到了我之前讨论的内容，这是非常技术性的深层内容，针对该工具的从业者的个人贡献者。 (00:59:20)：通过这个过程，我们与这些演讲者建立了这些关系，我们的倡导者帮助他们塑造他们的演讲。然后我认为我们确实通过这个过程和通过 Config 产生了非常强大的技术内容。我们还能够与与我们一起工作的这些人一起，帮助他们发展自己的形象，这也有助于他们与我们保持更紧密的联系，帮助他们凭借自己的能力成为思想领袖。所以我认为我们能够吸引这么多不同的人，他们是从业者和 IC，因为我们不仅仅是把思想领导力摆在那里。我们直接讨论如何使用该工具以及个人贡献者仍在处理的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's kind of a lot like this podcast and my newsletter. It's like how to actually do stuff, not just a bunch of big ideas. Claire Butler (01:00:03) Really. Yeah, no fluff.

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: Yep. Yep.

turns.en: Cool. All right. How do you do that?

turns.en: All right, so again, I've got four things here and I'll list them out and then we can go through them. turns.en: Oh, Designer Advocate.

turns.en: Awesome. Let's get into it.
turns.zh: 惊人的。让我们开始吧。

turns.speaker: Claire Butler
turns.en: All right, cool. So the first one's making it, the products easy to try and share. So we talked about this a little bit, but if you go to figma.com today, it's very easy to sign up for a free account. I have a free account myself on my personal side for designing my house, which is a thing I used to before, but you just go and you can try the tool. And I think that's so important for us to allow someone to use it over time for a long time until they have confidence enough to be able to want to spread it within their organizations. But then it's also pretty easy to create a free team and share stuff with your organization. Once we implemented pricing, which was about two years after we launched, we had this thing called a starter team. (01:02:21): And this is actually something that was switched. We realized that wait a minute, that's hurting us. And so we switched it and now it's like you can have something like three files, but unlimited collaborators. And that was huge for us. And that's a place where you can see it in the metrics very clearly, where it's like, oh, this is really easy for people now to share before they have to start paying. This is huge. (01:03:01): And so then you get people to start using it for free with their teams and the teams get confidence in it before then they all have to start uploading it to their procurement team or whoever it is to start paying for it. So not introducing payment too fast and giving people that time to build that advocacy and to try it out with their teams, with people before they have to pay, I think is huge there.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。所以第一个已经成功了，产品很容易尝试和分享。我们对此进行了一些讨论，但是如果您今天访问Figma.com，注册一个免费帐户非常容易。我个人有一个免费帐户用于设计我的房子，这是我以前习惯的事情，但你只要去就可以尝试该工具。我认为这对我们来说非常重要，允许人们长期使用它，直到他们有足够的信心能够在他们的组织内传播它。但创建一个免费团队并与您的组织共享内容也非常容易。在早期，你只需分享一个链接就可以了，你可以使用该工具，一切都是免费的。一旦我们实施定价，大约是在我们推出两年后，我们就有了一个叫做启动团队的东西。 (01:02:21)：这实际上是被改变的。所以最初我们的入门团队的工作方式是，你可以拥有无​​限的文件，但只能与两到三个人协作，这就是入门团队，你想添加更多的人来协作，然后你就付费了。我们意识到等一下，这伤害了我们。所以我们改变了它，现在就像你可以拥有三个文件之类的东西，但协作者不受限制。这对我们来说意义重大。在那里你可以在指标中非常清楚地看到它，就像，哦，现在人们在开始付费之前很容易分享。这是巨大的。 (01:03:01)：然后你会让人们开始与他们的团队免费使用它，并且团队会对它充满信心，然后他们都必须开始将其上传到他们的采购团队或任何开始付费的人。因此，不要太快地引入付款方式，并让人们有时间进行宣传，并在他们必须付款之前与他们的团队一起尝试，我认为这很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good and important topic that I want to pull a thread on a little bit. So what you discovered there is you don't want to get in the way of the growth engine of the product. turns.zh: 嗯，我认为另一件有趣的事情也是如此，我想我说过这一点，但我们的很多事情都是如此，所以我们有几个层次。我们有免费层，然后有专业层，然后我们有组织层。免费套餐，免费套餐包括这个免费的首发团队。所以你可以这样做，访问figma.com，然后去做。 Pro 是全部输入信用卡，然后 org 是您与销售人员交谈。组织和企业，您与销售人员交谈。所以我认为另一个关键的事情是我们从专业人士那里得到了很多向组织的追加销售。因此，这也是你在 org 和 pro 中投入什么的一个想法。这是另一个决定，因为专业版也相对便宜，所以它的增长速度太快了，这对我们来说仍然非常重要，但我们大多数营销合格的销售线索（销售线索）可能来自专业版或免费版。 (01:05:11)：所以我们考虑的决定是，好吧，你想卖什么？从免费到专业的过程必须非常自然，因为没有任何人参与。所以他们必须自己做这件事。然后，当您从专业人士转向组织或企业时，更多的是关于组织和规模。这就是我们可以讨论的设计系统对话的来源。但这是我们真正为组织和企业建立索引的事情，说明为什么您希望从专业版升级到组织。这是一个多步骤的过程，但它也很好，因为您可以在建立对工具的信心的同时增加对产品的投资。

But he was never a salesperson. Never had a quota, doesn't live on the sales team. Technical expert who has such a deep passion, and a deep, deep, deep, deep understanding of the tool, that he would come in and just help explain the product to other designers. (01:09:08): And it goes back to that same theme that I talked about earlier with marketing, where I realized that I would never have the credibility with designers that a designer has. Same is true with sales. They're never going to know the product as well as a designer will. Or "Here's where you're blocked," or "Here's an idea or best practice how to use this." (01:09:34): That just became so powerful and so useful for them and for the sales team, that they ended up calling it the Tom Factor, [inaudible 01:10:15]. turns.zh: 他确实没有一个组织可以带来它。他只是喜欢这个产品。但是 Tom，他是他公司的内部拥护者，他让他的公司采用 Figma。所以，当他加入 Figma 时，这确实是他带来的心态，就像“你如何将这个作为一个团队来使用？” (01:08:42)：我认为这如此特别，而且如此基础，以至于他们一起开始，是因为他们会一起与用户交谈，并将他带入销售流程。但他从来都不是推销员。从来没有配额，也不住在销售团队中。技术专家拥有如此深厚的热情，并且对工具有着深刻、深刻、深刻、深刻的理解，他会进来帮助向其他设计师解释产品。 (01:09:08)：这又回到了我之前谈到的营销主题，我意识到我永远不会像设计师那样获得设计师的信任。销售也是如此。他们永远不会像设计师那样了解产品。 (01:09:21)：所以，汤姆在那里，汤姆能够说，“哦，我完全明白你在说什么，以及你的问题是什么。这就是它的工作原理。”或者“这就是你被阻止的地方”，或者“这是如何使用它的想法或最佳实践。” (01:09:34)：这对他们和销售团队来说变得如此强大和有用，以至于他们最终将其称为 Tom Factor，[听不清 01:10:15]。因此，一开始它不一定是一个结构化的过程。他们只是想，“嘿汤姆，你能来帮助我们与这家公司交谈，或者帮助他们向他们展示这是如何运作的吗？” (01:09:51)：但后来他们称他为汤姆因素，因为他非常强大，如果他加入电话会议，他们的交易更有可能完成。但这也不是他的全职工作。他也与产品有联系。因为他是一个特殊的人，既是设计师，也是产品的[听不清 01:10:40] 用户，然后与数百名客户进行交谈。因此，他拥有综合产品反馈的最佳方法，然后将其带回产品团队，因为他拥有所有这些背景信息。所以，我认为这个角色非常特别，我们实际上选择扩大这个角色，因为它非常有价值。就像它对营销有价值一样，它对销售也有价值。
